t: The Nuragic people of Sardinia built the nuraghe, a stone tower with vaulted inner chambers, in large numbers from about 1800 BCE, and more than 7,000 still dot the island.
They were skilled metalworkers, among the main metal producers of Europe, and their pottery and bronzes reached the Aegean, Cyprus, Spain and the Etruscan cities of Italy.
Ancient DNA shows strong continuity with Sardinia’s Neolithic farmers and almost no steppe-related ancestry, unlike many other Bronze Age peoples of Europe.
dyk: The Giants of Mont’e Prama, stone statues up to 2.5 metres tall found near Cabras in 1974, have been dated between the 11th and 8th centuries BCE; if that is confirmed, they would be the oldest statues of people in the Mediterranean after those of Egypt.
ev: The first proto-nuraghi are built in the late Bonnanaro culture
The classic nuraghe, a tower with tholos chambers, evolves from the proto-nuraghe
Nuragic pottery reaches Tiryns, Kommos and Cyprus along the sea routes to the eastern Mediterranean
The building of new nuraghi stops
Phoenicians begin to visit Sardinia more often, as the Iron Age era of the aristocracies begins
A Carthaginian expedition under Malchus against a still strongly Nuragic Sardinia fails
Carthage surrenders Sardinia to Rome during the Mercenary War
The Giants of Mont’e Prama are found near Cabras

f.homeland: The island of Sardinia, with about one nuraghe every three square kilometres; key sites Su Nuraxi at Barumini, Santu Antine at Torralba, Nuraghe Losa, Nuraghe Arrubiu at Orroli, the sanctuary of Santa Vittoria at Serri, the holy well of Santa Cristina at Paulilatino, Mont’e Prama near Cabras
f.period: Bonnanaro culture and the first proto-nuraghi (c. 1800–1600 BCE); the classic nuraghi from the middle of the 2nd millennium BCE; no new nuraghi after the 12th–11th century BCE; the Iron Age “era of the aristocracies” (900–500 BCE); Carthaginian conquest of the coasts in the 6th century BCE; Roman rule from 238 BCE, with survival in the interior at least into the early Imperial period
f.known: the nuraghi, stone towers with vaulted tholos chambers; holy wells for a water cult; giants’ graves; the bronze statuettes called bronzetti; the Giants of Mont’e Prama; copper and bronze metalwork traded across the Mediterranean
f.sources: Excavations of nuraghi, villages, sanctuaries and tombs (Giovanni Lilliu’s synthesis of 1966 and later work); Nuragic pottery and bronzes found abroad; Greek and Roman writers such as Pseudo-Aristotle, Diodorus Siculus, Strabo and Justin; ancient DNA (2020 and later); no written records but a few possible short inscriptions
